text: Silver is clean. Now comes the aggregation that everything up to this point exists to make correct: collapsing one row per sale line item down into one row per calendar day.

This groups silver dot sales transactions by sale date, sums sales amount into total sales amount, counts distinct order ids into order count, and writes the result as gold dot daily sales summary. Notice sum gets imported under the alias underscore sum, because sum is also a built-in Python function, and shadowing it would cause confusing bugs later in the same notebook.

That countDistinct choice is not a style preference, it's a correctness requirement. Silver has one row per sale line item, so one order with three products on it produces three rows sharing the same order id. Counting rows would report three orders when there was really one. Counting distinct order ids counts each real order exactly once, which is what order count is actually supposed to mean.

The identical logic also works as plain Spark SQL — a create or replace table statement with the same group by, sum, and count distinct. Databricks and Fabric notebooks both let you mix PySpark and SQL cells freely, so recognizing both forms matters more than picking a favorite.

Gold is built — the one table this entire project was asked for. But before you trust it, you need to prove it's actually correct. Next lesson, you'll validate row counts across all three layers to catch exactly the kind of mistake a countDistinct oversight could have caused.
